title: Why Galaxies Stay Together

cues.text: A galaxy is a massive collection of stars, gas, and dust, all held together by the gravity of everything we can see.
If you calculate the gravity based only on that visible light,
outer stars should move slowly, or they would fly off into space.
But we see the opposite; those outer stars are whipping around the center at speeds that should tear the galaxy apart.
We think galaxies are embedded in a massive, spherical halo of dark matter,
an invisible substance that doesn't interact with light.
Even though we can't see it,
this halo contains far more mass than all the stars combined, creating a deep gravitational well.
This immense hidden weight provides the extra gravitational force needed to keep those fast outer stars tethered to the galaxy.
Just as the Sun's gravity keeps Earth in orbit,
dark matter acts as an invisible anchor, holding the entire structure together.
our galaxy would simply drift apart; dark matter is the silent glue that makes the galaxy possible.
It is this combined gravity of visible stars and the dark matter halo that keeps the outermost stars on their track.
